newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says 13 Japanese firms eye Natuna stake. [CORRECTED 09:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says 13 Japanese firms eye Natuna stake. [CORRECTED 09:40 GMT]

text.p: Thirteen Japanese companies have shown an interest in buying a stake from Indonesia's state-owned oil company Pertamina in the giant Natuna natural gas project, an Indonesian minister said on Tuesday.
Pertamina has a 24 percent stake in the gas project in the South China Sea but plans to reduce its share to 11 percent by selling 13 percent of the total stake.

"Thirteen Japanese companies intend to buy the stake from Pertamina. They have often come here to tell us they want to buy the stake...and they even want to buy it all if possible," State Minister of Research and Technology Jusuf Habibie told a news conference.
Habibie, chairman of the Natuna project team, said the companies involved included Japan National Oil Co (JNOC), Indonesia Petroleum Ltd (INPEX), Mitsubishi Corp, Mitsui & Co Ltd and Nisho Iwai Corp.
The Natuna project is 50 percent-owned by Exxon Corp, 26 percent by Mobil Corp and 24 percent by Pertamina (corrects Mobil's stake).
Habibie said the Indonesian government had asked the Japanese companies to divide the shares among themselves and said the government and the two U.S. firms would not interfere.
"We have asked JNOC to coordinate the division and I have learned they have divided the stake among them. The Indonesian government, Exxon and Mobil will not interfere," he added.
But Habibie said the companies had yet to reach a final agreement on the division as some of them were unhappy because their share was below one percent.

Habibie said there was also a request from the Petroleum Authority of Thailand to buy the shares, but the government decided that companies which were quick to sign the contract would receive their shares. He gave no other details.
The Natuna gas field is estimated to contain 210 trillion cubic feet (Tcf) of gas, of which 45 Tcf are thought to be commercially recoverable.
Habibie said the field would start producing five million tonnes of gas in 2002 and its capacity would increase to 15 million tonnes in the following three years.
